title: Why Ehud’s Assassination Still Feels Morally Uncomfortable
paragraphs: Why Ehud’s Assassination Still Feels Morally Uncomfortable
There are stories in Scripture we frame on walls.
David facing Goliath. Daniel in the lions’ den. Jesus calming the storm.
And then there are stories we quietly avoid.

Stories that make believers lower their voice. Stories that make skeptics raise their eyebrows. Stories that leave even mature Christians sitting in silence because they do not know what to do with what they just read.
Ehud is one of those stories.
A left-handed assassin. A hidden dagger. A private audience. A locked room. A king bleeding onto the floor. A nation celebrating afterward.
Judges 3 does not read like the sanitized Bible stories many people grew up hearing in children’s church. It reads almost disturbingly human.
And maybe that is exactly the point.

Because one of the greatest evidences that Scripture is true is that God did not airbrush human history. The Bible refuses to behave like propaganda. It preserves uncomfortable details. It records flawed people. It shows violence, betrayal, lust, cowardice, pride, political corruption, national collapse, and spiritual confusion.
The Bible does not hide humanity. It exposes it.
That is why Ehud’s assassination still unsettles people thousands of years later.

Not because the Bible is endorsing murder as morality. But because Judges is showing us what happens when humanity spirals into chaos while God still moves through broken history to preserve His covenant purposes.

And if we are honest… most people do not struggle with Ehud because they do not understand the text. They struggle because the story attacks modern assumptions about morality, justice, power, violence, and how God interacts with fallen societies.
It forces uncomfortable questions.

Can God use morally complicated people? Can divine judgment happen through political violence? Is descriptive history the same thing as divine approval? Why does Scripture preserve stories that feel ethically difficult? And why does this story still feel personal?
Because deep down, many people are wrestling with something even bigger:
“What do I do with a God who does not fit inside my preferred moral categories?”
The story begins during one of the darkest spiritual cycles in Israel’s history.

The Book of Judges repeatedly shows a terrifying pattern. Israel sins. Israel falls into oppression. Israel cries out. God raises a deliverer. Israel experiences temporary peace. Then the cycle begins again.
Judges is not a celebration of human righteousness. It is an autopsy of national collapse.
The Hebrew phrase repeated throughout Judges becomes one of the saddest refrains in Scripture:
“בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל”
“Bayyamim hahem ein melekh beYisrael.”
“In those days there was no king in Israel.”
And the conclusion becomes even more devastating:
“אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה”
“Ish hayashar be’einav ya’aseh.”
“Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
That line is not freedom. It is judgment.
Modern culture often imagines moral autonomy as liberation. Judges portrays it as societal decay.
When Israel abandoned covenant faithfulness, they did not become enlightened. They became fragmented. Violent. Spiritually numb. Politically unstable.
That context matters. Because if you read Ehud’s story disconnected from Judges as a whole, you can completely misunderstand what the text is doing.
This is not a simplistic hero story. This is covenant crisis literature.
The Moabite king Eglon oppressed Israel for eighteen years. The text intentionally highlights his dominance and Israel’s humiliation. Then Israel cried out to the Lord.
And Scripture says:
“וַיָּקֶם יְהוָה לָהֶם מוֹשִׁיעַ”
“Vayaqem Yahweh lahem moshi’a.”
“The LORD raised up for them a deliverer.”
The Hebrew word “מוֹשִׁיעַ” (moshi’a) means deliverer or savior. It comes from the same root connected to salvation.
But immediately, the story becomes strange.
The deliverer is Ehud. A left-handed man from the tribe of Benjamin.
That detail sounds insignificant to modern readers. It was not insignificant in the ancient world.
The Hebrew phrase is fascinating:
“אִטֵּר יַד־יְמִינוֹ”
“itter yad-yemino.”
Literally: “restricted in his right hand.”
Some scholars believe Ehud may have had a physical limitation. Others think the phrase simply identifies him as left-handed. Either way, the text intentionally highlights his difference.
And then comes the dagger.
Ehud forges a double-edged blade. Conceals it on his right thigh. Passes security because guards expected weapons on the opposite side. Then requests a private audience with the king.
What follows feels cinematic. Almost uncomfortably vivid.
The text says:
“וַיִּתְקַע הַדַּקֶר בְּבִטְנוֹ”
“Vayyitqa haddeqer bevitno.”
“And he thrust the dagger into his belly.”
The passage continues describing the blade disappearing into Eglon’s body. The doors locked. The servants waiting outside assuming the king was relieving himself. The delay. The panic. The discovery.
This is not sanitized storytelling.
And maybe that shocks people because many expect the Bible to behave like religious marketing.
But Scripture often refuses to flatter humanity.
The Bible records Noah getting drunk. Abraham lying. Moses disobeying. David committing adultery. Peter denying Christ. The disciples abandoning Jesus.
Biblical inspiration does not mean human beings become flawless. It means God tells the truth about them.
That distinction matters enormously.
One of the biggest mistakes people make while reading difficult Old Testament narratives is assuming that everything described is automatically prescribed.
But description is not always endorsement.
The Book of Judges repeatedly presents morally chaotic events precisely to show the consequences of spiritual rebellion.
In fact, as Judges progresses, the stories become increasingly horrifying. The nation deteriorates morally, politically, and spiritually. The book intentionally creates discomfort.
That discomfort is theological.
You are supposed to feel the instability. You are supposed to feel the tension. You are supposed to realize humanity cannot save itself.
Judges creates a longing for a righteous King.
And ultimately, that longing points beyond Israel’s failed leaders toward Christ.
Because every earthly deliverer in Judges is flawed. Every one.
Othniel. Ehud. Deborah. Gideon. Jephthah. Samson.
Some are courageous. Some are compromised. Some are tragic. Some are deeply broken.
The point is not: “Look how morally perfect these heroes are.”
The point is: “Look how desperately humanity needs redemption.”
And suddenly Ehud becomes less of a clean moral template and more of a mirror reflecting humanity’s fractured condition.
That is where the story starts feeling personal.
Because most people secretly want a God who only works through emotionally tidy situations.
But the Bible refuses to present history that way.
God works in prisons. Through exiles. Through betrayals. Through political collapse. Through imperfect people. Through messy history.
Not because He approves of all human behavior. But because His sovereignty is greater than human brokenness.
That tension makes people uncomfortable.
Especially modern readers shaped by simplified morality narratives.
But the ancient world was brutal. Empires enslaved nations. Kings crushed populations. Conquest involved horrifying violence.
The Bible is not pretending that world never existed. It enters it.
And yet even here, Scripture places moral boundaries around human violence. The Law condemned murder. The prophets rebuked bloodshed. Jesus later confronted hatred at the heart level itself.
So what do we do with Ehud?
We read carefully. Honestly. Humbly.

We recognize that God’s providence within history does not erase the moral complexity of human action. We avoid flattening the narrative into simplistic slogans. We refuse to weaponize the story to justify personal violence. And we remember that redemptive history unfolds progressively.
The Old Testament moves toward fulfillment in Christ.
And Jesus radically reframes how the people of God confront evil.
When Peter drew his sword in Gethsemane, Jesus said:
“ἀπόστρεψον τὴν μάχαιράν σου εἰς τὸν τόπον αὐτῆς”
“Apostrepson tēn machairan sou eis ton topon autēs.”
“Put your sword back into its place.”
Matthew 26:52.
Christ’s kingdom would not advance through assassination. It would advance through sacrificial love, truth, suffering, resurrection power, and Gospel proclamation.
That matters deeply.
Because some people read difficult Old Testament texts without recognizing the unfolding nature of biblical revelation.
The cross changes everything.
At Calvary, divine justice and divine mercy collided.
The sinless Son absorbed wrath that sinners deserved.
And suddenly the deepest shock of Scripture is no longer Ehud killing Eglon.
The deepest shock is God allowing Himself to be crucified by the very people He came to save.
That is the scandal at the center of Christianity.
Not merely judgment. But mercy.
Not merely wrath. But redemption.
Not merely justice. But grace poured onto the undeserving.
And maybe that is why Ehud’s story still lingers in people’s minds.
Because it exposes how desperately humanity longs for justice while simultaneously fearing what true justice would actually require.
Everyone wants evil judged. Until they realize they too stand guilty before a holy God.
Romans 3 destroys human self-righteousness:
“πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον”
“Pantes gar hēmarton.”
“For all have sinned.”
Not some. All.
The religious. The rebellious. The skeptic. The preacher. The addict. The proud. The secretly bitter. The publicly moral.
All.
Which means the real scandal is not that Scripture contains morally difficult stories.
The real scandal is that God continues offering mercy to morally difficult people.
People like us.
That is why the Bible refuses to flatten humanity into cartoon characters.
There are no purely clean heroes in Scripture outside of Christ.
And that honesty is one reason the Bible continues gripping people generation after generation.
Because it understands humanity better than humanity understands itself.
It understands the contradiction inside people.

The way someone can love and hate in the same hour. The way someone can worship publicly while hiding private compromise. The way entire societies can normalize evil while still believing themselves righteous.
Judges feels ancient. But it also feels terrifyingly current.
Because modern civilization still repeats the same pattern.
Moral autonomy. Spiritual drift. National confusion. Identity collapse. Political corruption. Violence. Self-worship.
“Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
That sentence could headline entire generations.
And yet into all that chaos, God still pursued people.
That is the heartbeat of Scripture.
Not humanity climbing upward toward God. But God pursuing fallen humanity again and again.
Even when people rebelled. Even when nations collapsed. Even when leaders failed. Even when hearts hardened.
And maybe someone reading this feels morally uncomfortable for another reason.
Because deep down, you know your own story is complicated too.
You know what it feels like carrying things you hope nobody discovers. You know what it feels like wrestling with regret. You know what it feels like trying to reconcile faith with your own failures.
That is why the Gospel matters.
Jesus did not come for polished people pretending to have no darkness. He came for sinners.
The Greek of Luke 5:32 is stunningly direct:
“οὐκ ἐλήλυθα καλέσαι δικαίους ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλοὺς εἰς μετάνοιαν”
“Ouk elēlytha kalesai dikaious alla hamartōlous eis metanoian.”
“I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
That word “μετάνοιαν” (metanoian) means repentance. A transformation of mind and direction. Not shallow guilt. Not performative religion. But genuine turning.
And maybe that is the hidden purpose behind difficult biblical stories.
They strip away shallow Christianity.
They force people to stop treating Scripture like decorative inspiration quotes.
They confront us with the reality of sin, judgment, human corruption, divine holiness, and the staggering necessity of grace.
Because if you never understand the depth of humanity’s brokenness, you will never fully understand the beauty of Christ’s redemption.
The Bible is not emotionally shallow. It is brutally honest. And because it is honest about human darkness, it becomes believable when it speaks about divine mercy.
That is why people still return to Scripture after exhausting themselves with motivational spirituality that never confronts the soul.
Only truth can heal what denial keeps alive.
And maybe somebody reading this has spent years trying to clean themselves up before approaching God.
You cannot save yourself.
That is the lesson echoing underneath all of Judges.
Human leaders fail. Human strength collapses. Human morality fractures. Human systems decay.
We need a greater Deliverer.
Not merely another judge. Not merely another political solution. Not merely another self-help strategy.
We need Christ.
The only perfectly righteous Judge. The only sinless Savior. The only King who conquers not through corruption, but through holiness.
And unlike Ehud, Jesus did not hide a blade under His garment.
He stretched out His hands and allowed nails to pierce them.
That is the Gospel.
The innocent dying for the guilty. The Holy One bearing sinners’ punishment. The Creator entering human suffering to rescue those who rebelled against Him.
And three days later, the tomb was empty.
That changes everything.
Because resurrection means evil does not ultimately win. Sin does not ultimately win. Death does not ultimately win.
Christ does.
So yes… Ehud’s assassination still feels morally uncomfortable.
It should.
Judges was never meant to leave readers comfortable with human nature.
It was meant to make us hunger for redemption.
And maybe that discomfort is exactly where some people finally stop trusting in themselves and start realizing how desperately they need Jesus.
And if this exposed something deeper than you expected, be honest about it. Somebody else reading your words may realize they are not alone.
Some people are not uncomfortable with Ehud because the Bible is broken. They are uncomfortable because Scripture refuses to lie about the darkness inside humanity.
